title: “Покинути все й почати життя з нуля”. Перемир'я в Олешках дотримується: що кажуть місцеві
content_c:
“Покинути все й почати життя з нуля”. Перемир'я в Олешках дотримується: що кажуть місцеві
  - Author, Відділ новин
  - Role, ВВС News Україна
- Published
- Час прочитання: 4 хв
Тимчасове перемир'я, встановлене в районі окупованого росіянами українського міста Олешки на Херсонщині почалось о 3 годині в ніч на 27 жовтня. Україна вказує, що станом на 17.30 27 жовтня Україна та Росія дотримуються домовленостей про режим тиші на визначених територіях, пов'язаних із проведенням гуманітарної місії.
Українська влада вказує, що режим припинення вогню поширюється на всю Херсонську область.
За оцінками українського уряду, від двох до шести тисяч цивільних мешканців опинилися там в блокаді та страждають від голоду.
Міноборони Росії підтвердило, що для проведення "гуманітарної операції" в районі Олешок припинили вогонь та ввели "режим тиші".
Українське командування напередодні теж підтвердило домовленість про тимчасове перемир'я.
ВВС поговорила з кількома місцевими мешканцями - тими, хто вже виїхав, і тими, хто ще там, - про настрої в місті.
Режим тиші
Український омбудсмен Дмитро Лубінець заявив, що режим тиші в Олешках запрацював в установлений час і зазначив, що сторони поки що дотримуються домовленостей.
Режим припинення вогню на Херсонському напрямку для евакуації з Олешок триватиме до 22:59 за місцевим часом у неділю, 1 листопада, повідомив голова фракції "Слуга народу" у Верховній Раді Давид Арахамія.
За його словами, це найбільша деескалація з 2022 року.
Що кажуть місцеві
Це перемир'я має дозволити доставити гуманітарну допомогу та очистити дороги від мін, щоб люди могли безпечно виїхати під час евакуації, запланованої на п'ятницю, 30 жовтня.
Одна жінка розповіла ВВС, що наступила на міну й наразі перебуває в лікарні, де перенесла дві операції.
"Я не знаю, скільки часу мені доведеться там провести", — сказала вона, хвилюючись, що не зможе приєднатися до евакуації.
Зв'язатися з людьми в Олешках складно, оскільки зв'язок працює зі збоями, а багато хто неохоче говорить про ситуацію через страх помсти з боку росіян. Це ускладнює перевірку повідомлень про те, чи дотримуються режиму припинення вогню.
Багато деталей планів евакуації залишаються незрозумілими, зокрема спочатку було невідомо, як і де для неї зареєструватися. Деякі люди хочуть знати, чи можуть вони взяти із собою домашніх улюбленців. Інші задаються питанням, яке майбутнє чекає на них, якщо вони вирішать залишити свої домівки.
Хоча люди оптимістично налаштовані щодо виїзду, є також побоювання, що Росія може не дозволити їм повернутися в Україну або перевірить їхні телефони й онлайн-активність на наявність ознак підтримки України. Це може призвести до їхнього викрадення та катувань.
Інший чоловік, з яким говорили журналісти BBC, підтвердив, що місцеві жителі бояться фільтрації. Особливо це стосується людей, які воювали в українській армії в період з 2014-2022 років. Він каже, що має знайомих, яких росіяни увʼязнювали за участь в АТО.
Чоловік зазначив, що якби евакуація відбувалася через річку, одразу на територію України, тоді би більше жителів погодилися на це.
Водночас співрозмовник зазначив, що деякі чоловіки не бажають виїжджати з Олешок, оскільки остерігаються, що їх одразу мобілізують до ЗСУ.
Він також розповів, що в морзі в Олешках перебуває понад 70 тіл і росіяни не дають дозволу їх поховати.
Журналісти BBC також поспілкувалися з жінкою, яка зв'язувалася зі своїми родичами та друзями, що досі залишаються в Олешках. Запитали їх, що вони думають про евакуацію, який там загальний настрій і як люди реагують на ситуацію.
Її знайомі зазначили, що бояться відновлення обстрілів під час евакуації, і що Україну якось звинуватять у недотриманні перемир'я.
"Ще одна серйозна проблема — це гроші та виживання після евакуації. Багато хто переймається тим, як жити далі, де знайти роботу і як забезпечити себе фінансово. Залишити все і починати життя з нуля в іншому місці — надзвичайно важко, особливо за нинішніх обставин", - розповіла вона.
Голод в Олешках
24 жовтня стало відомо, що перша леді США Меланія Трамп домоглася припинення вогню між Росією та Україною на окремій ділянці в окупованому місті Олешки. Про це йшлося у повідомленні Білого дому.
Згодом про тимчасове припинення вогню в Олешках також заявили у Генштабі ЗСУ та російському Генштабі.
"Ситуація в Олешках є критичною. Це прифронтове місто, яке стоїть на межі катастрофи. Населення, що залишилося в місті, складається переважно з людей похилого віку, які терміново потребують медичної допомоги, ліків, їжі та чистої води", - заявила Меланія Трамп, яку цитує пресслужба Білого дому.
Прифронтове місто вже багато місяців відрізане від постачання продуктів і ліків.
Раніше BBC спілкувалася з жителями окупованих Росією Олешок, які розповіли, як недоїдають, зокрема варять суп з бур'яну, і про те, яким небезпечним є виїзд з міста через заміновані дороги.
Український омбудсмен Дмитро Лубінець, який вів переговори з Меланією Трамп з української сторони, заявив, що операція з порятунку людей в Олешках максимально складна для реалізації.
"У рамках нашої угоди перше – буде забезпечено режим тиші. Друге – буде доставлений гуманітарний вантаж в Олешки. Третє – буде забезпечений вільне пересування цивільного населення з Олешок", – сказав він у своєму відео зверненні у телеграм.
Олешки опинилися в пастці як через географію, так і через війну.
Місто розташоване на лівому березі Дніпра, а на правому - Херсон. По прямій між ними дев'ять кілометрів, але зараз їх розділяє лінія фронту.
Херсон контролює Україна, а Олешки російські війська окупували ще у 2022 році. В 2023 році більша частина міста була затоплена через підрив армією РФ дамби Каховського водосховища.
description: В українській владі кажуть, що операція в Олешках почалася. Важливо, щоб вона пройшла "успішно та безпечно".

Зв'язатися з людьми в Олешках складно, оскільки зв'язок працює зі збоями, а багато хто неохоче говорить про ситуацію через страх помсти з боку росіян. Це ускладнює перевірку повідомлень про те, чи дотримуються режиму припинення вогню.
Багато деталей планів евакуації залишаються незрозумілими, зокрема спочатку було невідомо, як і де для неї зареєструватися. Деякі люди хочуть знати, чи можуть вони взяти із собою домашніх улюбленців. Інші задаються питанням, яке майбутнє чекає на них, якщо вони вирішать залишити свої домівки.
Хоча люди оптимістично налаштовані щодо виїзду, є також побоювання, що Росія може не дозволити їм повернутися в Україну або перевірить їхні телефони й онлайн-активність на наявність ознак підтримки України. Це може призвести до їхнього викрадення та катувань.
Інший чоловік, з яким говорили журналісти BBC, підтвердив, що місцеві жителі бояться фільтрації. Особливо це стосується людей, які воювали в українській армії в період з 2014-2022 років. Він каже, що має знайомих, яких росіяни увʼязнювали за участь в АТО.
Чоловік зазначив, що якби евакуація відбувалася через річку, одразу на територію України, тоді би більше жителів погодилися на це.
Водночас співрозмовник зазначив, що деякі чоловіки не бажають виїжджати з Олешок, оскільки остерігаються, що їх одразу мобілізують до ЗСУ.
Він також розповів, що в морзі в Олешках перебуває понад 70 тіл і росіяни не дають дозволу їх поховати.
Журналісти BBC також поспілкувалися з жінкою, яка зв'язувалася зі своїми родичами та друзями, що досі залишаються в Олешках. Запитали їх, що вони думають про евакуацію, який там загальний настрій і як люди реагують на ситуацію.
Її знайомі зазначили, що бояться відновлення обстрілів під час евакуації, і що Україну якось звинуватять у недотриманні перемир'я.
"Ще одна серйозна проблема — це гроші та виживання після евакуації. Багато хто переймається тим, як жити далі, де знайти роботу і як забезпечити себе фінансово. Залишити все і починати життя з нуля в іншому місці — надзвичайно важко, особливо за нинішніх обставин", - розповіла вона.
Голод в Олешках
24 жовтня стало відомо, що перша леді США Меланія Трамп домоглася припинення вогню між Росією та Україною на окремій ділянці в окупованому місті Олешки. Про це йшлося у повідомленні Білого дому.
Згодом про тимчасове припинення вогню в Олешках також заявили у Генштабі ЗСУ та російському Генштабі.
"Ситуація в Олешках є критичною. Це прифронтове місто, яке стоїть на межі катастрофи. Населення, що залишилося в місті, складається переважно з людей похилого віку, які терміново потребують медичної допомоги, ліків, їжі та чистої води", - заявила Меланія Трамп, яку цитує пресслужба Білого дому.
Прифронтове місто вже багато місяців відрізане від постачання продуктів і ліків.
Раніше BBC спілкувалася з жителями окупованих Росією Олешок, які розповіли, як недоїдають, зокрема варять суп з бур'яну, і про те, яким небезпечним є виїзд з міста через заміновані дороги.
Український омбудсмен Дмитро Лубінець, який вів переговори з Меланією Трамп з української сторони, заявив, що операція з порятунку людей в Олешках максимально складна для реалізації.
"У рамках нашої угоди перше – буде забезпечено режим тиші. Друге – буде доставлений гуманітарний вантаж в Олешки. Третє – буде забезпечений вільне пересування цивільного населення з Олешок", – сказав він у своєму відео зверненні у телеграм.
Олешки опинилися в пастці як через географію, так і через війну.
Місто розташоване на лівому березі Дніпра, а на правому - Херсон. По прямій між ними дев'ять кілометрів, але зараз їх розділяє лінія фронту.
Херсон контролює Україна, а Олешки російські війська окупували ще у 2022 році. В 2023 році більша частина міста була затоплена через підрив армією РФ дамби Каховського водосховища.

title: До п'яти зросла кількість постраждалих у Харкові через ворожий удар, серед них дитина – ДСНС
content_c:
Унаслідок нічного удару російського реактивного дрона по Основ'янському району Харкова поранено п'ятьох людей, серед них 4-річну дитину, повідомляє ДСНС України.
"Унаслідок атаки спалахнула масштабна пожежа на площі 2500 кв. м – горіли багатоквартирний та приватний житлові будинки, господарчі споруди й виробнича будівля", – йдеться в повідомленні служби в телеграмі.
Також пошкоджено багатоповерхівки, гаражі та автомобілі.
Рятувальники ліквідовують наслідки удару під загрозою повторних атак. Психологи ДСНС надали допомогу постраждалим.
Як повідомлялося, станом на 23:39 кількість постраждалих внаслідок російського удару по Основ'янському району Харкова зросла до 4,повідомив начальник обласної військової адміністрації Олег Синєгубов.

title: Mbappé sorry for 'ill-judged' Mao remark after backlash in China
content_c:
Mbappé sorry for 'ill-judged' Mao remark after backlash in China
- Published
Kylian Mbappé has apologised for "ill-judged" comments he made about late Chinese leader Mao Zedong which led to him being dropped by several Chinese brands.
Mbappé had reportedly told French talk show The Bridge the meme "that makes me laugh the most, it's the one where there's a video of a guy, I think it's a Chinese dictator..." He then laughs as the clip cuts to a meme showing his face superimposed on an image resembling Mao.
The meme is part of a running joke about the Real Madrid forward being called a "dictator" because of his huge influence in football.
"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world," Mbappé said in a statement.
"I apologise to everyone my words have upset."
Spain's La Liga also apologised, saying it "deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappé's recent comments have caused among Chinese fans".
The joke did not go down well in China, where Mao is revered by the Communist Party, despite his chaotic and often violent rule that left millions dead.
A few people came out in support of him on Chinese social media, but that is a rare response given China's tightly controlled internet, where people are expected to toe the party and government line on sensitive topics.
Few topics are as sensitive as Mao, which may explain why brands were so quick to terminate partnerships with a global sports star like Mbappé.
The original video is not available on the show's YouTube channel, and it's unclear when the interview hosted by Real Madrid's Aurélien Tchouaméni first aired. In clips that have been circulating online, Mbappé does not identify Mao by name. He says he "uses [the meme] with friends all the time".
The furore appeared to kick off on Monday night after Chinese football forum Dongqiudi drew attention to the comments in a statement, saying they were "inappropriate" and "hurt the feelings of Chinese people".
Screengrabs of the clip and meme have since spread quickly on Chinese social media, with people echoing this sentiment and even calling for a boycott of both the French striker and his club, Real Madrid.
But some have blurred the meme itself as well as the part of the comment they found offensive, when Mbappe refers to "a Chinese dictator".
Dongqiudi said in its statement that it was "unable to translate" his comments because they were "offensive to China and the Chinese people".
Many people are therefore also wondering what exactly Mbappe said and have responded to the angry posts and comments with questions, wanting to know more.
What is the reaction in China?
Chinese fans have been criticising Mbappé – who is popular in China and has huge brand endorsements – of "profiting from the Chinese market yet making remarks that offend the Chinese public".
"International public figures, in particular, should show greater respect and sensitivity, as national sentiment must never be taken lightly," reads another comment on Weibo.
As the anger online grew louder, Chinese brands began to cut ties, although they did not explicitly refer to the video.
The country's largest dairy producer, Mengniu, said it "firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people".
Drinks giant Dongpeng issued a similar statement: "Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments."
According to state-owned newspaper The Global Times, state broadcaster CCTV's news apps will not feature content related to the French striker. CCTV will also stop showing La Liga matches, Chinese media reported on Tuesday. Real Madrid is one of 20 clubs that play in the Spanish football league and is the most decorated team with 36 league titles.
China's foreign ministry has also weighed in, with spokesperson Lin Jian saying: "We have noted the relevant reports. Words and deeds that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with opposition from all sectors of Chinese society."
China is a major market for international sports stars and homegrown brands have signed multimillion-dollar endorsement contracts with Mbappé, Norwegian striker Erling Haaland, and NBA player Stephen Curry.
By 14:00 local time on Tuesday, five of the top 10 trending topics on Weibo centered on Mbappé, with the hashtag "multiple brands terminate partnerships with Mbappé" topping the list.
"Don't ever come to China," read one of the top comments on Weibo.
Why is Mao a sensitive topic?
Mao founded the People's Republic of China in 1949 and ruled through tumultuous decades in the 1960s and 1970s.
His attempt at rapid industrialisation, which he called the Great Leap Forward, led to a famine that killed tens of millions. Then came the Cultural Revolution: a violent purge of anyone seen as a threat to Communism, which included Chinese intellectuals, landowners, artists and often rivals within the Party.
His death in 1976 brought a new era for China, which began to open its doors to the global economy. Even as the country moved away from Mao's rule, he continued to be hailed by the party as a national icon whose legacy was beyond reproach.
So jokes or memes about Mao are seen not just as an insult to the party but also its closely-guarded narrative about the country's past.
It's unclear when the Mbappé meme involving Mao began but his nickname, "the dictator", has made the striker the subject of many memes and jokes online.
Mbappé is widely regarded as one of the best footballers in the world and has wielded significant influence at the clubs he has played for. His extraordinary speed, goalscoring ability and worldwide popularity have made him a global icon, attracting millions of fans, major sponsorship deals and media attention, with his influence extending into fashion, culture and business.
In 2024, he sued a French influencer and kebab shop owner for using his name in the description of one of the shop's sandwiches, leading to more jokes about the nickname.
France teammate Ousmane Dembele jumped on the trend during the 2026 World Cup, calling Mbappé Mobut – a reference to Mobutu Sese Seko, the dictator who ruled the Democratic Republic of Congo, formerly Zaire, for three decades.
In an interview with France Football in September, Mbappé acknowledged the light-heartedness behind many of these memes, but said they "sometimes reveal a lack of political and human awareness among people".
"There's a side that's a bit less funny, because we know the damage people like that have caused throughout history," he said.
"Being compared to people who murder others, or who have made millions upon millions of people miserable... I don't think I've done that in my life."
Additional reporting by Fan Wang and Osmond Chia

title: UK and EU officials to discuss freedom of movement
content_c:
UK and EU officials to discuss freedom of movement
- Published
British and European officials will discuss the future options for the UK's relationship with the EU, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds has told the BBC.
Officials on both sides are expected to begin discussions about a range of options, including free movement, before the EU summit on 20 November.
However, Downing Street has insisted the government's current focus is on achieving new deals in areas such as food and youth mobility at the summit.
Reynolds said no "assumptions" had been made about what the UK's future relationship with Brussels could look like.
Andy Burnham has said he wants an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and EU.
But the prime minister has been clear any major changes to the UK-EU relationship would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.
He has vowed to stick by the red lines in Labour's 2024 manifesto, with no return to freedom of movement, the EU single market or customs union, for the duration of this parliamentary session, which will end by 2029.
Freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country, is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market.
The single market enables goods, services and people to move freely between member states, with countries also applying many common rules and standards.
- Chris Mason: Burnham faces crunch decisions in his next 100 days 
  - Published1 day ago
- Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement 
  - Published1 day ago
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Reynolds said current discussions ahead of the summit are around food and drink, electricity and emissions trading.
He said: "What the prime minister has also said, quite rightly, is we face a series of policy changes on the European side that will affect us.
"We need to get as little uncertainty as possible, we need to have a way to resolve what our long-term relationship will be and he is going to set that out after the summit.
"He is going to be frank with the British people about what the trade-offs are but no assumptions have been made on that."
Pressed on whether UK officials are talking to the EU about freedom of movement Reynolds said: "They will be talking to them about what the future options for our relationship might be.
"But here and now, the focus should be on the summit and the tangible difference improvements we're going to make."
A government spokesperson stressed there were no current discussions on freedom of movement.
"We are working with the EU on the areas set out and agreed ahead of the UK-EU Summit and within the manifesto red lines," the spokesperson added.
Burnham is far more willing to have a public conversation around Brexit than his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, whose government was nervous about reopening a debate that proved so contentious in the past.
Some people within the Labour Party had been urging Sir Keir to go further and there is a widely held view that Burnham's comments are likely to go down well with voters tempted by the Liberal Democrats and Greens.
But there is nervousness among Labour MPs with small majorities in Brexit-supporting, Reform-facing constituencies.
Labour MP Melanie Onn, whose constituency Great Grimsby and Cleethorpes backed leaving the EU, told the Today programme Burnham risked losing trust by talking about going beyond the 2024 manifesto at a future election.
"I don't think that the scars have healed for many people around the country so I do think this is an unnecessary conversation to be having at this time," she said.
Onn, who lost her seat in 2019 to the Conservatives but won it back in 2024, warned against re-opening the conversation, saying: "Trust is incredibly important, it's hard-earned and easily lost, and on this matter I think that we should tread incredibly carefully."
Speaking to BBC Wales, Labour MP Ruth Jones said: "We need to be very careful here. We must respect the Brexit referendum result."
Asked if a referendum on freedom of movement was something she would support, the MP for Newport West and Islwyn said: "We're a long way from that. Andy Burnham is floating the idea, and it's great to float ideas, but let's talk it through and see what does it mean, because another referendum at this particular time would be divisive."
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage told BBC Breakfast that "Andy Burnham has no mandate to be in Brussels, to be negotiating any of this" and called for the prime minister to put his ideas to the public in a general election.
On Monday, Burnham left the door open to a potential referendum on freedom of movement with the EU.
The prime minister caused some confusion when he told broadcasters that he would not reintroduce free movement without a referendum, but Downing Street later said no decisions had been made on whether a public vote would be needed.
Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told the BBC on Sunday that no options for the UK's future relationship could be taken off the table.
But Burnham did appear to draw some red lines of his own when he told the Sunday Times, external that he would not be in favour of the UK joining the euro or the border-free Schengen zone.
The fact the prime minister has not been willing to say the same thing about free movement is being seen in Westminster as evidence that he believes it is a genuine option.

He has vowed to stick by the red lines in Labour's 2024 manifesto, with no return to freedom of movement, the EU single market or customs union, for the duration of this parliamentary session, which will end by 2029.
Freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country, is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market.
The single market enables goods, services and people to move freely between member states, with countries also applying many common rules and standards.
- Chris Mason: Burnham faces crunch decisions in his next 100 days 
  - Published1 day ago
- Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement 
  - Published1 day ago
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Reynolds said current discussions ahead of the summit are around food and drink, electricity and emissions trading.
He said: "What the prime minister has also said, quite rightly, is we face a series of policy changes on the European side that will affect us.
"We need to get as little uncertainty as possible, we need to have a way to resolve what our long-term relationship will be and he is going to set that out after the summit.
"He is going to be frank with the British people about what the trade-offs are but no assumptions have been made on that."
Pressed on whether UK officials are talking to the EU about freedom of movement Reynolds said: "They will be talking to them about what the future options for our relationship might be.
"But here and now, the focus should be on the summit and the tangible difference improvements we're going to make."
A government spokesperson stressed there were no current discussions on freedom of movement.
"We are working with the EU on the areas set out and agreed ahead of the UK-EU Summit and within the manifesto red lines," the spokesperson added.
Burnham is far more willing to have a public conversation around Brexit than his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, whose government was nervous about reopening a debate that proved so contentious in the past.
Some people within the Labour Party had been urging Sir Keir to go further and there is a widely held view that Burnham's comments are likely to go down well with voters tempted by the Liberal Democrats and Greens.
But there is nervousness among Labour MPs with small majorities in Brexit-supporting, Reform-facing constituencies.
Labour MP Melanie Onn, whose constituency Great Grimsby and Cleethorpes backed leaving the EU, told the Today programme Burnham risked losing trust by talking about going beyond the 2024 manifesto at a future election.
"I don't think that the scars have healed for many people around the country so I do think this is an unnecessary conversation to be having at this time," she said.
Onn, who lost her seat in 2019 to the Conservatives but won it back in 2024, warned against re-opening the conversation, saying: "Trust is incredibly important, it's hard-earned and easily lost, and on this matter I think that we should tread incredibly carefully."
Speaking to BBC Wales, Labour MP Ruth Jones said: "We need to be very careful here. We must respect the Brexit referendum result."
Asked if a referendum on freedom of movement was something she would support, the MP for Newport West and Islwyn said: "We're a long way from that. Andy Burnham is floating the idea, and it's great to float ideas, but let's talk it through and see what does it mean, because another referendum at this particular time would be divisive."
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage told BBC Breakfast that "Andy Burnham has no mandate to be in Brussels, to be negotiating any of this" and called for the prime minister to put his ideas to the public in a general election.
On Monday, Burnham left the door open to a potential referendum on freedom of movement with the EU.
The prime minister caused some confusion when he told broadcasters that he would not reintroduce free movement without a referendum, but Downing Street later said no decisions had been made on whether a public vote would be needed.
Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told the BBC on Sunday that no options for the UK's future relationship could be taken off the table.
But Burnham did appear to draw some red lines of his own when he told the Sunday Times, external that he would not be in favour of the UK joining the euro or the border-free Schengen zone.
The fact the prime minister has not been willing to say the same thing about free movement is being seen in Westminster as evidence that he believes it is a genuine option.

title: China's families are now supporting more old people than kids
content_c:
China's families are now supporting more old people than kids
- Published
Families in China are for the first time supporting more elderly people than children, the country's government has said.
Official data released in the last week, external show the ratio of China's dependent elderly people compared to the working age population rose to 23% last year, overtaking the figure for children, which stood at 22%.
The numbers are closely watched for signs of how China's shrinking workforce will impact both the world's second largest economy and global growth as a whole.
The latest figures mark a significant milestone as China grapples with an ageing population that could have implications for families, pensions and healthcare spending, analysts say.
China has been preparing for a growing proportion of elderly people in recent years, while urging younger generations to get married and for couples to have more children.
The latest data from China's National Bureau of Statistics show there are now more than 223 million people in China aged 65 and above, accounting for nearly 16% of the country's total population.
At the same time there are about 213 million children aged 14 and under.
No official commentary was published with the statistics. But Chinese state-controlled news outlet Global Times wrote that the nation's "entry into a moderately ageing society" is the result of a mix of factors, including the "size of past birth cohorts" and longer life expectancy.
The shift could place added strain on pension, healthcare and long-term care systems, while also creating opportunities in the so-called silver economy that caters to older consumers, the newspaper said.
"It reflects a historical trend in demographic development rather than a short-term phenomenon," Global Times quoted one researcher as saying.
The demographic shift is "symbolic" and could suggest more public spending will move from families and schools to pensions and healthcare, said Professor Stuart Gietel-Basten from The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.
It may also pose a challenge to the country's ambitions, as it could limit its economic growth as well as people's spending power, said National University of Singapore sociology lecturer Mu Zheng.
China's ageing population has been driven by a mix of factors, including rapid urbanisation and the effects of the controversial one-child policy, which was in place from 1980 to the end of 2015.
The strategy, designed to keep China's rapid population growth under control, is estimated by the country's government to have prevented about 400 million births since it began, though this number has been contested.
The policy played a key role in shrinking the population and means there are fewer younger people to support a growing number of elderly relatives, Mu said.
But despite easing restrictions on the size of families, Beijing has struggled to persuade couples to have more children, with birth rates hitting historic lows.
Other contributing factors include changing gender roles, rising living costs and higher education levels that have put pressure on fertility rates, Mu said.
Beijing made further support for older people a part of the measures in its five-year economic blueprint that was announced earlier this year.
Financial help for pensioners has been a growing part of Chinese government spending. More than 53 million elderly people were receiving senior citizen allowances and subsidies by the end of 2025, according to official figures.
The Global Times noted that many people entering old age who were born between the 1950s and the 1970s have generally higher incomes compared to previous generations, stronger purchasing power and are healthier.
The dependency ratio is widely-used to measure ageing populations but it has also been questioned by some experts who argue that its scope is too limited.
Gietel-Basten said the use of the statistics risks "taking agency away" from older people - many of whom he says have been misrepresented as dependants.
It also does not take into account improvements to healthcare, he added.

title: Flávio Bolsonaro flees Brazil after presidential election loss, reports say
content_c:
The far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro has reportedly fled Brazil and is on his way to the United States after losing Sunday’s presidential election to the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who called the act “shameful”.
A report by the news website Metrópoles, citing people close to the politician’s family, said he was en route to the US. “The plane is in flight,” Metrópoles reported, without making clear where it had departed from.
Bolsonaro allies told Metrópoles that he would land in Florida on Tuesday afternoon and planned to request political asylum. “The Donald Trump administration has been informed,” the website added.
Lula condemned Bolsonaro’s apparent decision to flee. “This is what the family Bolsonaro are like. Brazil is their second homeland. Their first homeland is licking the boots of the US, as he’s become accustomed to doing,” he said at an event celebrating his 81st birthday in Brasília.
“I keep imagining what’s on the conscience of a citizen who just lost the elections and flees his country … He who owes nothing, fears nothing. A citizen who sneaks out of his country owes something. The act of leaving Brazil is shameful.”
Allies also confirmed to the Folha de S Paulo newspaper that Bolsonaro was on his way to the US, and said the escape plan had been “organized and enabled by a lawyer close to the Bolsonaro clan”.
“They say the flight should land in a few hours,” the newspaper added.
The news network CNN Brasil reported that Bolsonaro had fled to the US with his wife and two daughters in the early hours of this morning.
A US state department spokesperson said Bolsonaro and his family would be granted visas “to allow them entry into the United States”.
Lawmakers from Lula’s Workers’ party asked the supreme court to order Bolsonaro’s arrest and requested that his name be put on Interpol’s Red Notice list.
Bolsonaro had not been seen since Monday and missed a Tuesday-morning deadline to hand his passport to the federal police, fuelling rumours that he may have fled Brazil after losing on Sunday.
A report in the Brazilian newspaper O Globo said that during a meeting with friends and lawyers on Monday, the defeated candidate had appeared “possessed and made it clear he was afraid of being arrested”.
A supreme court justice cancelled Bolsonaro’s passport minutes after the result in a ruling related to a criminal case against the senator. He had until 11am to surrender the document to the federal police, but did not appear.
Bolsonaro has had Italian citizenship since 2023 and reportedly possesses a passport from the European country.
The Argentinian news website Infobae reported that on Monday night he reportedly fled to Argentina, where he was expected to board a private jet in Puerto Iguazú bound for the US, but the plane did not take off.
Bolsonaro, who has yet to concede defeat to Lula, posted a video on Monday in which, commenting on the cancellation of his passport, he said: “I never thought about leaving the country.”
One of the senator’s brothers, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, who is in self-imposed exile in the US, had said in an interview last Friday that his brother should leave Brazil if he lost.
The Brazilian newspaper Folha de S Paulo reported that allies in the Bolsonaro family’s inner circle had been told that he had indeed left for Argentina and intended to travel from there to the US.
As there is no record of him passing through any regular Brazilian immigration checkpoint, the federal police are trying to establish from Argentinian authorities whether there is any record of him entering the country.
The Argentinian channel Todo Noticias reported that the senator had reportedly crossed the border into Argentina on foot and abandoned plans to board the plane once news of his movements leaked.
Bolsonaro was told to surrender his passport over a criminal case in which the federal police are investigating him for possible involvement in a money-laundering scheme worth about £680m ($905m) involving betting companies.
The senator’s possible flight makes the future of the far right after the presidential election even more uncertain. The family patriarch, Jair Bolsonaro, is under house arrest for attempting a coup, and one of his sons is in the US and the whereabouts of another unclear.
Eduardo Bolsonaro has an outstanding arrest warrant against him in Brazil, after being sentenced to four years in prison for trying to interfere in his father’s trial by lobbying Donald Trump to impose sanctions on the justices hearing the case.
Political scientist Magna Inácio, a professor at the Federal University of Minas Gerais, believes a power vacuum may now emerge within the right.
“The resistance of Brazilian voters to handing victory to this more extremist camp sends a signal that the right leadership is now up for grabs,” she said.
Since Jair Bolsonaro, then a career congressman with few laws to his name, surprisingly won the presidency in 2018, there has effectively been no right wing in Brazil, only the far-right Bolsonarismo movement.
Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right, believes the fact that three Bolsonaros are now potentially out of the picture could trigger a “shift in power” away from blood ties.
“I think there is a tendency for power to move away from the sons,” said Rocha, noting that before the election, polls showed Jair Bolsonaro supporters preferred other potential candidates over his eldest son, including Jair Bolsonaro’s wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, who was recently elected senator, and the São Paulo governor, Tarcísio de Freitas.
Flávio Bolsonaro reportedly did not want to run because he thought a presidential campaign would turn his life into “hell”, and believed his re-election to the senate was assured. But with Eduardo, his father’s “plan A”, now living in the US, the senator was chosen to run.
Most observers agree that Flávio lacks his father’s charisma. He had a 24-year political career in which he passed very few laws as a state legislator and senator, and the only previous time he ran for executive office was for mayor of Rio de Janeiro in 2016, when he fainted during a televised debate and finished fourth.
Speaking in Brasília, Bolsonaro’s campaign chief, senator Rogério Marinho, said he was surprised by reports of his candidate’s departure. “Because yesterday we talked about the need for Flávio, with the 60 million votes he received, to take on this role as leader of the opposition … since we were given a mandate by a significant part of the population,” he said.
Asked whether he believed Bolsonaro could lead the opposition from abroad, he said: “María Corina Machado did it” with her country, Venezuela.
Even in a family frequently embroiled in legal trouble he stood out, facing longstanding criminal allegations, including suspicions that he embezzled part of his staff’s salaries, as well as more recent accusations.
Even so, 48.21% of Brazilians voted for Flávio Bolsonaro on Sunday, which many analysts see as both an anti-Lula vote and a vote for whomever Jair Bolsonaro had chosen.
Inácio believes the struggle over the Bolsonaro legacy will also play out among family members who remain in Brazil, including Michelle and Bolsonaro’s other political sons, the senator-elect Carlos Bolsonaro and congressman-elect Jair Renan Bolsonaro, who publicly do not get along with their stepmother.
“Michelle clearly has a political project of her own, but she is likely to face strong resistance from the two stepsons who are in congress. It is only a matter of time before tensions between them grow,” said the political scientist.

title: Labour faces accusations of breaking manifesto pledge over minimum wage for young people – as it happened
content_c:
Labour faces accusations of breaking manifesto pledge over minimum wage for young people – as it happened
Greens say Labour has ‘no respect for young people’ amid reports chancellor will pause equalisation of minimum wage for under-21s with that paid to older workers
Greens accuse Labour of breaking manifesto pledge, after minister signals minimum wage age equalisation being paused
Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, has not contested reports saying that, in the budget tomorrow, John Healey, the chancellor, will pause the process of equalising the lower national minimum wage paid to people under the age of 21 with the more generous national living wage that applies to older workers.
In an interview on the BBC this morning, Reynolds was asked to respond to a story suggesting the equalisation process has been put on hold because of concerns about youth unemployment.
John Healey will announce plans to increase the minimum wage by nearly 4% but slow the rise for young people after warnings that they are being priced out of jobs.
The Times has been told that the national living wage, which applies to those aged 21 and over, is expected to rise from £12.71 to around £13.20 – an increase of 3.9%.
However, Healey has decided not to repeat the big rises of the past two budgets in the national minimum wage, which applies to those aged 18 to 21. It will rise broadly in line with the rate for older workers – from £10.85 to around £11.27, an increase of 3.9%.
In its manifesto, Labour said it would raise the level of the national minimum wage to the level of the national living wage to “so all adults are entitled to the same minimum wage, delivering a pay rise to hundreds of thousands of workers across the UK”. The manifesto implied this would happen during this parliament, but in May Torsten Bell, the pensions minister, said implementation of this commitment could be delayed until after the general election – implying the government is worried equalisation now could increase youth unemployment.
Asked about the Times story on the Today programme, Reynolds insisted the new national living wage and national minimum wage rates would be announced tomorrow.
But he went on:
The manifesto pledge on equalisation still applies, but it was always clear it would happen over time and we would take into account, as the minimum wage uprating each year always does, the relative strength of the labour market and other pressures …
Of course, you want not just good wages, but good work. And the way this has always been done – it is a balance of making sure the pressures on the labour market are taken into account. That is the approach you will see confirmed [in the budget].
The Green party has accused Labour of breaking a manifesto promise. Responding to the Times’ story, and Reynolds’ comments in effect confirming it, Mothin Ali, the Greens’ co-deputy leader, said:
Anyone doing a day’s work, needs to be paid the same rate for the same job. A young person’s rent and food bill is no less because they are young, so they need to receive the same wage.
Healey and Burnham are now breaking a manifesto pledge to young people that even Starmer managed to keep. Labour have no respect for young people, who appear to just be there for cheap labour for the wealthy and their corporate donors.
Ali said the Greens would introduce a £15 minimum wage for workers of all ages.
Labour has been accused of breaking a manifesto pledge to raise the minimum wage for younger people up to the level that applies to workers over the age of 21 after a minister signalled that the process of equalising the two different rates will be paused in the budget. (See 12.52pm.)
Bridget Phillipson, the Labour chair, has said Nigel Farage is “completely unfit for public office” after the Reform UK leader in interviews this morning said he would not block a candidate for liking Tommy Robinson (see 12.13pm) and refused to condemn a former aide who called Kemi Badenoch a Nigerian scammer. In response, Phillipson said:
Nigel Farage is desperately trying to drag politics further and further into the gutter. It seems there is no low he won’t stoop to – he is completely unfit for public office.
Failing to call out blatant racism against the leader of His Majesty’s Opposition despite being given at least ten opportunities to do so and then giving his activists the green light to support Tommy Robinson shows just who he really is.
For a full list of all the stories covered on the blog today, do scroll through the list of key event headlines near the top of the blog.
Minister opens National School of Government and Public Services
A National School of Government and Public Services has opened, the Cabinet Officehas announced. Mark Ferguson, a Cabinet Office minister, formally opened it today. The government says:
Regional hubs will be developed across the country, with the first opened in York this week, alongside digital access routes to give civil servants access to modern learning facilities close to where they live and work.
It will provide civil servants and public sector leaders with the world-class learning and development they need to meet the challenges of the future.
The school will build a curriculum around the skills all servants need, including training on devolution, national security, leadership and innovation. Training will also be offered in AI, covering the full range of skills needed now and in the future, from implementing practical solutions at the frontline to cut clerical workloads to cloud engineering courses to develop and deploy the latest technology across government, the School will equip Civil Servants with the tools to build a world-class Civil Service.
Security minister says Britons far less ready for emergencies than other Europeans as he defends Be Ready campaign
Last week the government launched a Be Ready campaign to publicise advice saying people should stockpile water, food and other supplies in the event of an emergency. The announcement attracted a lot of attention, although many Britons probably sided with Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, who signalled that she was not going to get too alarmed by it all by joking about how she would include a bottle of sauvignon blanc and mascara alongside her government-mandated survival supplies.
Dan Jarvis, the security minister, gave a statement about the advice to MPs this afternoon. In his opening comments, he did not pass judgment on the usefulness or otherwise of a bottle of wine, but he did have some points to add.
Jarvis dismissed claims that the advice was an “overreaction”. Anyone who did think that should have been with him when he met victims of Storm Goretti earlier this year, he said. He said 50,000 homes, schools and businesses were left without power, communities were cut off because of blocked roads and families experienced having “the basic necessities of everyday life”, like power, water and the internet, taken away from them.
He said government research shows only 13% of people in the UK feel they are prepared for an emergency, like having power cut off after a storm. He went on:
This figure is far lower than our European neighbours. The very same research showed that 84% of people in the UK want the government to share more information about the steps they can take to increase their preparedness.
He said the last government launched a website giving preparedness guidance, but there was no proper publicity campaign and “not enough people noticed [the advice], and those who did found the guidance hard to follow”.
He said the publicity campaign was not being launched in response to a specific threat.
He said there were two main things people are being asked to do.

Asked about the Times story on the Today programme, Reynolds insisted the new national living wage and national minimum wage rates would be announced tomorrow.
But he went on:
The manifesto pledge on equalisation still applies, but it was always clear it would happen over time and we would take into account, as the minimum wage uprating each year always does, the relative strength of the labour market and other pressures …
Of course, you want not just good wages, but good work. And the way this has always been done – it is a balance of making sure the pressures on the labour market are taken into account. That is the approach you will see confirmed [in the budget].

title: Experts urge 'global health emergency' as climate harms accelerate
content_c:
Experts urge 'global health emergency' as climate harms accelerate
October 28, 2026
As heat deaths, drought and food insecurity accelerate worldwide, nearly 150 researchers from more than 30 countries are calling for climate change to be declared a "global health emergency."
The health and economic toll of planetary heating has risen sharply in the decade since countries signed the Paris climate accord — a landmark deal to stop climate change that was hailed by the World Health Organization (WHO) at the time as "the most important public health agreement of the century."
Yet, climate change was responsible for more than half a million heat deaths in 2023 alone and nearly 3 million since 2016. The area affected by extreme drought, which threatens food and water supplies and raises the risk of disease, grew more than 700% faster than in the decade before. And heat cost the world an estimated $1.07 trillion in lost potential income last year, all according to the annual Lancet Countdown on Health and Climate Change.
"This cannot continue," said Alan Dangour, director of climate and health at Wellcome Trust, one of the world's largest charities, which funded the Lancet report. "We must change course and put the health and well-being of people at the heart of our response to climate change — measuring success not through emissions targets or degrees Celsius but by lives saved and health outcomes improved."
Climate-linked health harms growing faster than before
The latest findings from the Lancet study show how rapidly the health risks are growing by comparing this decade to the one before the Paris Agreement was signed.
Heat is the starkest example. Climate change was responsible for 68% of heat-related deaths between 2016 and 2023, up from 55% in the previous decade. The yearly increase in climate-driven heat deaths more than doubled over the same period.
But deaths are only "the tip of the iceberg," said Ollie Jay of the University of Sydney's Heat and Health Research Center. "Except that iceberg is not melting, it's growing every year." Beneath the surface are also heatstroke, lost sleep, and worsening chronic health conditions.
The economic harms are mounting too. Working in extreme heat puts people at risk of heat exhaustion, illness or injury and, ultimately, losing income and livelihoods.
Heat wiped out 573 billion potential working hours in 2025, with farmworkers bearing the brunt. Vulnerable economies in Africa and South-East Asia were hit hardest with losses reaching 5% of GDP, compared with 0.5% in the more developed economies.
"The economic toll is battering vulnerable sectors and communities the hardest," Marina Romanello, executive director of the Lancet Countdown, who is based at University College London, told journalists at a press briefing.
Water extremes are intensifying too. Satellite data show that since 2003, 43% of the world's land has been steadily drying out, while 37% has been getting wetter. Together, that is more than 80% of land shifting to extremes that threaten crops, food supplies, and sanitation.
Drought can leave people without safe drinking water and raises the risk of infectious disease, while floods bring drowning, injury and contaminated water.
Heat waves and droughts pushed nearly 128 million more people into food insecurity in 2024, compared with the 1981–2010 average.
"This isn't a gradual worsening; it's a step change," Romanello said.
What would declaring a global health emergency change?
To save lives and protect human health, experts are calling for a new WHO instrument to help countries share information, coordinate responses, monitor threats, and disburse funds. The United Nations and its member states would create the mechanism.
The closest existing version of this is the WHO's Public Health Emergency of International Concern mechanism (PHEIC) used during the COVID-19 pandemic and mpox outbreaks. But built with short-term emergencies in mind, it falls short of addressing a complex threat that requires sustained global action across multiple sectors, like climate change.
The world needs a broader approach, "so that we're not responding to emergency after emergency," said Romanello. "We're doing a cohesive long-term response that builds resilience, builds capacities and builds the possibilities of countries to avoid further emergencies."
Progress happening but not nearly fast enough
Romanello told journalists that "we have more than enough proof" that such action does improve health outcomes. "Early warning systems informed by climate, have already seen a reduction in the adverse impacts of these extreme weather events," she said.
The growth in renewable energy has also partly aided a reduction in deaths from fossil fuel air pollution in half of 140 countries assessed since 2016, preventing an estimated 323,000 deaths a year.
And 56 countries now have national plans to adapt their health services for climate impacts, such as heat waves and disease outbreaks, up from just 14 in 2015.
But progress remains too slow, according to the report.
Fossil fuels, the burning of which releases emissions fueling planetary heating as well as other pollutants, still supply more than 80% of the world's energy.
Energy-related emissions hit a record high in 2024. The world's 100 largest oil and gas companies are on track to produce 150% more oil and gas by 2040 than is compatible with limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit). A year ago, that figure was 138%.
Investing in an old technology
Governments continue to fund fossil fuels, with net subsidies doubling since 2016 to $6.2 trillion. In 2024, 10 countries spent more on such subsidies than on their entire health systems.
Yet as fossil fuel prices rise and renewables become cheaper, these polluting technologies are becoming increasingly uneconomical, said Romanello.
Romanello likened new fossil fuel investment to "investing in Blockbuster when you have Netflix," — a bet on an old technology, referring to the once ubiquitous video rental store that failed to adapt to streaming.
Meanwhile, money to help health systems adapt to climate change is scarce. Developing countries estimate they need around $3.3 billion a year for such adaptations, which the Lancet authors say is likely an underestimate. Only about a third of that was committed in 2024. Foreign aid reductions, led by the US and followed by Germany, which made the second-largest cut, are widening the gap.
"This report is a stark warning that climate change is a health emergency," said Helen Clark, former prime minister of New Zealand and chair of the Lancet Countdown's board. "What's missing is not evidence, but the political will to act on it."

description: Heat, drought and storms linked to climate change are already killing millions worldwide. Researchers want global warming to be declared a global health emergency as the health harms from it escalate faster than ever.
content:
Experts urge 'global health emergency' as climate harms accelerate
October 28, 2026
As heat deaths, drought and food insecurity accelerate worldwide, nearly 150 researchers from more than 30 countries are calling for climate change to be declared a "global health emergency."
The health and economic toll of planetary heating has risen sharply in the decade since countries signed the Paris climate accord — a landmark deal to stop climate change that was hailed by the World Health Organization (WHO) at the time as "the most important public health agreement of the century."
Yet, climate change was responsible for more than half a million heat deaths in 2023 alone and nearly 3 million since 2016. The area affected by extreme drought, which threatens food and water supplies and raises the risk of disease, grew more than 700% faster than in the decade before. And heat cost the world an estimated $1.07 trillion in lost potential income last year, all according to the annual Lancet Countdown on Health and Climate Change.
"This cannot continue," said Alan Dangour, director of climate and health at Wellcome Trust, one of the world's largest charities, which funded the Lancet report. "We must change course and put the health and well-being of people at the heart of our response to climate change — measuring success not through emissions targets or degrees Celsius but by lives saved and health outcomes improved."
Climate-linked health harms growing faster than before
The latest findings from the Lancet study show how rapidly the health risks are growing by comparing this decade to the one before the Paris Agreement was signed.
Heat is the starkest example. Climate change was responsible for 68% of heat-related deaths between 2016 and 2023, up from 55% in the previous decade. The yearly increase in climate-driven heat deaths more than doubled over the same period.
But deaths are only "the tip of the iceberg," said Ollie Jay of the University of Sydney's Heat and Health Research Center. "Except that iceberg is not melting, it's growing every year." Beneath the surface are also heatstroke, lost sleep, and worsening chronic health conditions.
The economic harms are mounting too. Working in extreme heat puts people at risk of heat exhaustion, illness or injury and, ultimately, losing income and livelihoods.
Heat wiped out 573 billion potential working hours in 2025, with farmworkers bearing the brunt. Vulnerable economies in Africa and South-East Asia were hit hardest with losses reaching 5% of GDP, compared with 0.5% in the more developed economies.
"The economic toll is battering vulnerable sectors and communities the hardest," Marina Romanello, executive director of the Lancet Countdown, who is based at University College London, told journalists at a press briefing.
Water extremes are intensifying too. Satellite data show that since 2003, 43% of the world's land has been steadily drying out, while 37% has been getting wetter. Together, that is more than 80% of land shifting to extremes that threaten crops, food supplies, and sanitation.
Drought can leave people without safe drinking water and raises the risk of infectious disease, while floods bring drowning, injury and contaminated water.
Heat waves and droughts pushed nearly 128 million more people into food insecurity in 2024, compared with the 1981–2010 average.
"This isn't a gradual worsening; it's a step change," Romanello said.
What would declaring a global health emergency change?
To save lives and protect human health, experts are calling for a new WHO instrument to help countries share information, coordinate responses, monitor threats, and disburse funds. The United Nations and its member states would create the mechanism.
The closest existing version of this is the WHO's Public Health Emergency of International Concern mechanism (PHEIC) used during the COVID-19 pandemic and mpox outbreaks. But built with short-term emergencies in mind, it falls short of addressing a complex threat that requires sustained global action across multiple sectors, like climate change.
The world needs a broader approach, "so that we're not responding to emergency after emergency," said Romanello. "We're doing a cohesive long-term response that builds resilience, builds capacities and builds the possibilities of countries to avoid further emergencies."
Progress happening but not nearly fast enough
Romanello told journalists that "we have more than enough proof" that such action does improve health outcomes. "Early warning systems informed by climate, have already seen a reduction in the adverse impacts of these extreme weather events," she said.
The growth in renewable energy has also partly aided a reduction in deaths from fossil fuel air pollution in half of 140 countries assessed since 2016, preventing an estimated 323,000 deaths a year.
And 56 countries now have national plans to adapt their health services for climate impacts, such as heat waves and disease outbreaks, up from just 14 in 2015.
But progress remains too slow, according to the report.
Fossil fuels, the burning of which releases emissions fueling planetary heating as well as other pollutants, still supply more than 80% of the world's energy.
Energy-related emissions hit a record high in 2024. The world's 100 largest oil and gas companies are on track to produce 150% more oil and gas by 2040 than is compatible with limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit). A year ago, that figure was 138%.
Investing in an old technology
Governments continue to fund fossil fuels, with net subsidies doubling since 2016 to $6.2 trillion. In 2024, 10 countries spent more on such subsidies than on their entire health systems.
Yet as fossil fuel prices rise and renewables become cheaper, these polluting technologies are becoming increasingly uneconomical, said Romanello.
Romanello likened new fossil fuel investment to "investing in Blockbuster when you have Netflix," — a bet on an old technology, referring to the once ubiquitous video rental store that failed to adapt to streaming.
Meanwhile, money to help health systems adapt to climate change is scarce. Developing countries estimate they need around $3.3 billion a year for such adaptations, which the Lancet authors say is likely an underestimate. Only about a third of that was committed in 2024. Foreign aid reductions, led by the US and followed by Germany, which made the second-largest cut, are widening the gap.
"This report is a stark warning that climate change is a health emergency," said Helen Clark, former prime minister of New Zealand and chair of the Lancet Countdown's board. "What's missing is not evidence, but the political will to act on it."
Edited by: Jennifer Collins

title: Knesset-Wahl in Israel: Prognosen zeigen Patt-Situation in Israel
content_c:
Wahl in Israel Prognosen zeigen Patt-Situation in Israel
Nach der Wahl in Israel sehen mehrere TV-Sender ein enges Rennen um die Mehrheit im Parlament. Sowohl Eisenkot als auch Netanjahu kündigten an, eine Regierung bilden zu wollen.
Aktualisierte Prognosen vom frühen Mittwoch der führenden israelischen TV-Sender zeigen nach der Wahl in Israel eine Patt-Situation zwischen dem rechtsreligiösen Lager des Ministerpräsidenten Benjamin Netanjahu und dem ebenfalls aus mehreren Parteien bestehenden Lager seines Hauptrivalen Gadi Eisenkot.
Die Sender Channel 13 und Kan sahen das Netanjahu-Lager bei 51 von 120 Sitzen im Parlament, ebenso wie das Lager um Ex-Militärchef Gadi Eisenkot.
Laut den Prognosen wird Netanjahus rechtskonservative Likud-Partei mit 27 Mandaten stärkste Kraft im Parlament, auf Platz zwei kommt Eisenkots Mitte-Partei Jaschar mit 21 bis 22 Mandaten. Der TV-Sender N12 sieht die Likud-Partei bei 24 und die Jaschar-Partei bei 22 Sitzen. Nur der TV-Sender C14, der als Sprachrohr Netanjahus gilt, sieht eine klare Mehrheit von 62 der 120 Mandate für das Lager des Ministerpräsidenten.
Die Parteien der arabisch-israelischen Staatsbürger schnitten deutlich besser ab als erwartet. Sie kommen laut Nachwahlbefragungen auf einen Rekord von 17 bis 18 Sitzen - was der Opposition theoretisch den Weg an die Macht ebnen könnte. Allerdings hatte Eisenkot bislang nicht öffentlich erklärt, dass er mit den überwiegend arabischen Listen zusammenarbeiten würde.
Beide wollen Regierung bilden
Der israelische Oppositionsführer Eisenkot kündigt an, eine neue Regierung bilden zu wollen. Die Menschen in Israel hätten sich für "den Wandel entschieden", er werde versuchen, eine neue Regierung zu bilden, sagte Eisenkot am frühen Mittwochmorgen in einer Rede vor seinen Anhängern in Tel Aviv. Netanjahus Koalition habe "das Vertrauen des Volkes verloren". Den amtierenden Regierungschef warnte er davor, "Israels Sicherheit für Ihre politischen Zwecke zu missbrauchen".
Netanjahu will eine "starke" neue rechtsgerichtete Regierung bilden. Seine rechtskonservative Likud-Partei sei "die größte Partei Israels" und das rechte Lager habe innerhalb der jüdischen Bevölkerung eine klare Mehrheit, sagte er vor Anhängern. Netanjahu hielt seine Rede gegen 03.00 Uhr morgens (Ortszeit, 02.00 Uhr MEZ). Anders als für ihn üblich, fasste er sich diesmal kurz. Er erklärte sich zwar nicht ausdrücklich zum Wahlsieger, verwies jedoch darauf, dass seine Likud-Partei voraussichtlich als stärkste Einzelkraft aus der Wahl hervorgehen werde. Zudem sprach er sich gegen jede "Regierung mit der Unterstützung der israelischen Araber" aus.
Hohe Wahlbeteiligung
Mit Schließung der Wahllokale um 21:00 Uhr lag die Wahlbeteiligung bei 77,7 Prozent und damit dem höchsten Stand seit mehr als zwei Jahrzehnten. Das entspricht 5.695.682 Wählerinnen und Wählern.
Die Prognosen basieren auf Befragungen von Wählern direkt nach ihrer Stimmabgabe am Wahllokal. Wie alle Umfragen unterliegen auch diese sogenannten Exit-Umfragen einer gewissen Fehlerquote. Vorläufige Ergebnisse werden in den kommenden Stunden erwartet. Die endgültigen Ergebnisse werden in den kommenden Tagen erwartet und können von den Exit-Umfragen abweichen.

title: Nach der Niederlage von Langzeit-Herrscher Aleksandar Vucic bei den Parlamentswahlen hofft Serbiens Medienwelt auf einen Neuanfang
content_c:
Nach Vucics Niederlage hofft Serbiens Medienwelt auf Neuanfang
27. Oktober 2026
Keine 24 Stunden nach dem Wahlsieg der Studierendenliste Serbiens über die bislang allmächtige Serbische Fortschrittspartei (SNS) begann der Moderator einer öffentlich-rechtlichen Nachrichtensendung mit einem Eingeständnis:
"Es wurde verschwiegen, ein Auge zugedrückt, einseitig informiert, unkritisch berichtet. Die richtigen Fragen wurden nicht gestellt - oder überhaupt keine Fragen. Und dafür schulden wir den Zuschauern eine Entschuldigung", so Goran Eror, Sprecher einer Sendung, die der öffentlich-rechtliche Rundfunk der nordserbischen Provinz Vojvodina (RTV) produziert, die aber auch vom gesamt-serbischen Rundfunk RTS ausgestrahlt wird.
Eror und andere Kollegen hatten jahrelang innerhalb des bisherigen Systems gekämpft - mit wenig Erfolg. Nun trat der Chefredakteur von RTV auf Druck der Gewerkschaft zurück. Ähnliches fordern Beschäftigte jetzt auch bei RTS. Der größere öffentlich-rechtliche Sender, der Kritik an der Regierung jahrelang ignoriert hatte, hat seinen Ton seit dem Sieg der Studentenliste am vergangenen Sonntag (25.10.2026) nur ein Stück weit geändert.
Gewalt gegen Sprachrohr der bisherigen Regierung
Ein paar Stunden später, am Montagabend, drang eine Gruppe aufgebrachter Bürger in den Belgrader Fernsehsender Informer ein. Der gilt als Sprachrohr der bisherigen Regierung. Die Eindringlinge sollen Geräte zerstört und das Programm zeitweise unterbrochen haben. "Sie wollten mich töten", klagte Chefredakteur Dragan J. Vucicevic.
Informer führt seit Jahren eine ganze Schar von Boulevardmedien an, die Regierungskritiker als "Verräter", "Terroristen" und "Ustascha" brandmarken. Als Ustascha wurden die kroatischen Faschisten bezeichnet, die während der Zeit des Nationalsozialismus Völkermord an Serben, Juden und Roma begingen.
Ein Präsident, der immer auf Sendung war
Das sind nur einige der Folgen des politischen Erdbebens vom vergangenen Sonntag, bei dem Aleksandar Vucic, der als Präsident und Ministerpräsident fast 15 Jahre lang allgegenwärtig war und Serbien mit harter Hand regierte, die politische Macht in Serbien verloren hat. Die Studierendenliste, auf der Professoren, Aktivisten und Künstler stehen, gewann 141 der 250 Parlamentssitze. Vucics SNS erhielt 103 Mandate.
Geschlagen wurde der Langzeit-Herrscher derart deutlich von einer Wahlliste, die Studierende nach zweijährigem Protest zusammengestellt hatten. Die Proteste hatten nach dem Einsturz des Vordachs am frisch renovierten Bahnhof von Novi Sad Ende 2024 begonnen. 16 Menschen starben. Es besteht der Verdacht auf Korruption und Pfusch bei den Bauarbeiten.
Kritiker prangern seit Jahren Vetternwirtschaft und Verbindungen zwischen Staat und organisierter Kriminalität in Serbien an. Und sie verwiesen immer wieder auf die Medienmaschinerie, die Vucic auf Schritt und Tritt begleitete - und auf der seine Dominanz beruhte.
In den vergangenen Jahren wandte sich Vucic im Durchschnitt mehr als einmal täglich an die Öffentlichkeit: auf langen Pressekonferenzen oder in Livesendungen. Kundgebungen seiner Partei wurden mitunter von rund vierzig TV-Sendern gleichzeitig übertragen.
Wie einseitig die Berichterstattung war, zeigen Zahlen des unabhängigen Büros für Sozialforschung BIRODI. In den letzten Wochen des Wahlkampfs wurde Vucic auf fünf landesweit empfangbaren Fernsehsendern in 96 Prozent der Beiträge positiv dargestellt. Die Studierendenliste dagegen kam in 95 Prozent der Fälle schlecht weg.
Kein Wunder, dass viele Bürger nun wütend und ungeduldig sind. "Ich erwarte zunächst, dass sich die Gemüter beruhigen. Denn die Unzufriedenheit der Bürger mit jenen Medien ist groß, die Propagandisten der Regierung und von Hassrede waren - und keine Journalisten", sagt Aleksandra Krstic, die an der Fakultät für Politikwissenschaften in Belgrad Mediensysteme lehrt.
"Mit dem Eindringen in ein Medium löst man überhaupt nichts. Die Regulierungsbehörde für elektronische Medien sollte ein Verfahren zum Entzug der Sendelizenz einleiten. Das ist der einzige Weg", so Krstic gegenüber der DW. Auch diese Behörde wurde in den Jahren der Herrschaft von Vucic und seiner SNS mit regierungstreuen Mitarbeitern besetzt. Das dürfte sich mit dem neuen Parlament ändern.
Milliarden für Kabel, Sport und regierungsnahe Sender
Der staatliche Telekomkonzern investierte im Laufe der Jahre mehr als zwei Milliarden Euro: in kleinere Kabelanbieter, in Übertragungsrechte für Sportveranstaltungen, die ein großes Publikum anziehen - und in die direkte Finanzierung Dutzender regierungsnaher Fernsehsender.
Erst kürzlich kaufte der portugiesische Fonds Alpac Capital, Eigentümer von Euronews, einige der letzten regierungskritischen Medien in Serbien. Es folgten Entlassungen von Redaktionsleitern und Druck auf Journalisten, ihre Kritik unmittelbar vor der Wahl abzuschwächen.
Damit könnte nun Schluss sein. Im Wahlprogramm der Studierendenliste steht, dass der staatliche Telekomkonzern "nicht Eigentümer von Fernseh- oder Radiosendern oder Onlineportalen sein darf, die Nachrichtenprogramme produzieren". Fernsehsender, die die Bürger informieren, sollen zudem über alle Kabelanbieter empfangbar sein.
"Unsere Hoffnung ist, dass jene zur Verantwortung gezogen werden, die Medien für Propaganda missbraucht haben, und jene, die das mit dem Geld der Bürger bezahlt haben", sagt Stevan Ristic, Geschäftsführer der unabhängigen Wochenzeitung Vreme und Vorsitzender des serbischen Medienverbandes, eines großen Zusammenschlusses von Medienverlagen.
"Außerdem hoffen wir, dass es keine privilegierten Medien mehr geben wird. Das würde die Medienlandschaft bereinigen und die unabhängigen Medien endlich in die Lage versetzen, auf einem freien Markt zu bestehen, auf dem Werbegelder ehrlich verdient werden, statt dass Werbung an genehme Medien gelenkt wird. Kurz gesagt: dass die Gesetze eingehalten werden", sagt Ristic der DW.
description: Regierungsnahe Sender dominierten 15 Jahre lang die Öffentlichkeit Serbiens. Seit dem Wahlsieg der Studentenliste wächst die Hoffnung auf mehr Medienfreiheit und eine Aufarbeitung der Propaganda.

Das sind nur einige der Folgen des politischen Erdbebens vom vergangenen Sonntag, bei dem Aleksandar Vucic, der als Präsident und Ministerpräsident fast 15 Jahre lang allgegenwärtig war und Serbien mit harter Hand regierte, die politische Macht in Serbien verloren hat. Die Studierendenliste, auf der Professoren, Aktivisten und Künstler stehen, gewann 141 der 250 Parlamentssitze. Vucics SNS erhielt 103 Mandate.
Geschlagen wurde der Langzeit-Herrscher derart deutlich von einer Wahlliste, die Studierende nach zweijährigem Protest zusammengestellt hatten. Die Proteste hatten nach dem Einsturz des Vordachs am frisch renovierten Bahnhof von Novi Sad Ende 2024 begonnen. 16 Menschen starben. Es besteht der Verdacht auf Korruption und Pfusch bei den Bauarbeiten.
Kritiker prangern seit Jahren Vetternwirtschaft und Verbindungen zwischen Staat und organisierter Kriminalität in Serbien an. Und sie verwiesen immer wieder auf die Medienmaschinerie, die Vucic auf Schritt und Tritt begleitete - und auf der seine Dominanz beruhte.
In den vergangenen Jahren wandte sich Vucic im Durchschnitt mehr als einmal täglich an die Öffentlichkeit: auf langen Pressekonferenzen oder in Livesendungen. Kundgebungen seiner Partei wurden mitunter von rund vierzig TV-Sendern gleichzeitig übertragen.
Wie einseitig die Berichterstattung war, zeigen Zahlen des unabhängigen Büros für Sozialforschung BIRODI. In den letzten Wochen des Wahlkampfs wurde Vucic auf fünf landesweit empfangbaren Fernsehsendern in 96 Prozent der Beiträge positiv dargestellt. Die Studierendenliste dagegen kam in 95 Prozent der Fälle schlecht weg.
Kein Wunder, dass viele Bürger nun wütend und ungeduldig sind. "Ich erwarte zunächst, dass sich die Gemüter beruhigen. Denn die Unzufriedenheit der Bürger mit jenen Medien ist groß, die Propagandisten der Regierung und von Hassrede waren - und keine Journalisten", sagt Aleksandra Krstic, die an der Fakultät für Politikwissenschaften in Belgrad Mediensysteme lehrt.
"Mit dem Eindringen in ein Medium löst man überhaupt nichts. Die Regulierungsbehörde für elektronische Medien sollte ein Verfahren zum Entzug der Sendelizenz einleiten. Das ist der einzige Weg", so Krstic gegenüber der DW. Auch diese Behörde wurde in den Jahren der Herrschaft von Vucic und seiner SNS mit regierungstreuen Mitarbeitern besetzt. Das dürfte sich mit dem neuen Parlament ändern.
Milliarden für Kabel, Sport und regierungsnahe Sender
Der staatliche Telekomkonzern investierte im Laufe der Jahre mehr als zwei Milliarden Euro: in kleinere Kabelanbieter, in Übertragungsrechte für Sportveranstaltungen, die ein großes Publikum anziehen - und in die direkte Finanzierung Dutzender regierungsnaher Fernsehsender.
Erst kürzlich kaufte der portugiesische Fonds Alpac Capital, Eigentümer von Euronews, einige der letzten regierungskritischen Medien in Serbien. Es folgten Entlassungen von Redaktionsleitern und Druck auf Journalisten, ihre Kritik unmittelbar vor der Wahl abzuschwächen.
Damit könnte nun Schluss sein. Im Wahlprogramm der Studierendenliste steht, dass der staatliche Telekomkonzern "nicht Eigentümer von Fernseh- oder Radiosendern oder Onlineportalen sein darf, die Nachrichtenprogramme produzieren". Fernsehsender, die die Bürger informieren, sollen zudem über alle Kabelanbieter empfangbar sein.
"Unsere Hoffnung ist, dass jene zur Verantwortung gezogen werden, die Medien für Propaganda missbraucht haben, und jene, die das mit dem Geld der Bürger bezahlt haben", sagt Stevan Ristic, Geschäftsführer der unabhängigen Wochenzeitung Vreme und Vorsitzender des serbischen Medienverbandes, eines großen Zusammenschlusses von Medienverlagen.
"Außerdem hoffen wir, dass es keine privilegierten Medien mehr geben wird. Das würde die Medienlandschaft bereinigen und die unabhängigen Medien endlich in die Lage versetzen, auf einem freien Markt zu bestehen, auf dem Werbegelder ehrlich verdient werden, statt dass Werbung an genehme Medien gelenkt wird. Kurz gesagt: dass die Gesetze eingehalten werden", sagt Ristic der DW.

title: РФ розривають нові вибухи: у Новомосковську горить хімзавод, росіяни у паніці, місту загрожує хімзабруднення (фото, відео)
content_c:
РФ розривають нові вибухи: у Новомосковську горить хімзавод, росіяни у паніці, місту загрожує хімзабруднення (фото, відео)
Вночі проти 28 жовтня Росію розривали вибухи. До міста Новомосковськ Тульської області “завітали” безпілотники. Місцеві жителі панікували через навалу дронів, скаржилися на вибухи і сильну пожежу.
Що відомо про атаку - читайте на сайті ТСН.ua.
Уночі в Тульській області РФ оголосили ракетну та безпілотну небезпеку. Місцеві жителі повідомляли про вибухи, після яких в кількох районах Новомосковська виникли пожежі.
У Новомосковську під прицілом опинився хімічний завод «Азот”. На території підприємства виникла пожежа. Губернатор Тульської області Дмитро Міляєв підтвердив атаку на регіон, мовляв, сили ППО працюють по БпЛА. Втім, начебто «інфраструктуру у прилеглій промисловій зоні” пошкодили уламки збитих дронів.
За даними OSINT-ресурсів і різних Telegram-каналу Exilenova+, зайнялася установка з виробництва аміаку «Ам-70». На кадрах у мережі видно сильну пожежу і стовпи диму, що затягують місто.
Місцева влада закликає мешканців зберігати спокій. Водночас до міста вже направили лабораторії регіонального управління Росспоживнагляду, які мають перевірити рівень можливого хімічного забруднення.
Що відомо про завод “Азот”
Завод «Азот» входить до групи «ЄвроХім» і є одним із найбільших виробників азотних добрив у Росії. На підприємстві виготовляють аміак, аміачну селітру, карбамід і метанол.
Водночас завод має значення не лише для хімічної промисловості РФ. За даними Служби зовнішньої розвідки України, підприємство постачало азотну кислоту заводу імені Свердлова в Дзержинську, який виробляє вибухові речовини для російського військово-промислового комплексу.
